response.text:
Evidence supports mutation testing as guidance, but does not establish recommender mutation scores as calibrated predictors of real implementation bugs. Mao et al.’s [2024 IST study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2024.107410) evaluates six metamorphic relations across LibRec, PREA and Surprise, reporting failures and ranking relations/libraries. This supports relational testing’s feasibility; observed violations alone do not establish confirmed implementation defects or improved debugging decisions. Full text was inaccessible, so exact fault operators, tolerance selection, independent evaluation mutations, runtime overhead and confirmed bug fixes could not be verified from the accessible abstract/excerpts. These details should remain unverified rather than inferred.

Stronger, indirect evidence comes from conventional software. [Just et al.](https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/fse_2014_just.pdf) studied 357 real faults and 230,000 mutants: detection correlated after controlling for coverage; 73% of faults were coupled to mutants, while 10% required stronger/new operators and 17% exposed inherent limitations. However, [Papadakis et al.](https://coinse.github.io/publications/pdfs/Papadakis2018hi.pdf) found weak correlations after controlling for test-suite size, despite significantly better real-fault detection among higher-scoring, equally sized suites. Thus, mutation scores can guide test improvement without accurately predicting bug-detection probability; neither result directly validates sequential-recommender audits.

For the proposed audit, incremental value requires comparison against existing checks using confirmed bugs and held-out mutation operators. Candidate operators include padding/readout errors, target leakage, item-index shifts and checkpoint/predictor mismatches. Select tolerances on correct implementations, freeze them before evaluation, and report false alarms, incremental bugs detected, localization/repair success and GPU overhead including retraining. These are evaluation recommendations, not established findings. A [systematic ML-testing review](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-020-09881-0) warns that unrealistic mutations and invalid transformations weaken synthetic-fault validity. Assessment: plausible potential and feasible implementation; novelty and debugging benefit remain conditional on independent evidence beyond mutation coverage.
